chapter_title: Advanced System Monitoring and Performance Tuning
chapter_summary:
Effective system administration at an RHCA level demands more than just knowing basic commands; it requires a deep understanding of how to diagnose and resolve subtle performance bottlenecks that can cripple applications, especially in cloud and DevOps environments where resource efficiency is paramount. We begin our journey by diving into a suite of powerful RHEL tools designed for granular system monitoring and performance analysis. These tools move beyond simple `top` or `free` output, providing insights into kernel-level activities, process interactions, and resource utilization patterns.

One of the most potent tools in your arsenal is `perf`, a Linux profiling tool built directly into the kernel. Unlike user-space tools, `perf` can capture hardware performance counters, kernel events, and user-space function calls with minimal overhead. To begin profiling, you might use `perf record -g -a sleep 10` to record system-wide activity for 10 seconds, including call graphs. After recording, `perf report` will present an interactive view of the most CPU-intensive functions, allowing you to drill down into specific processes or even kernel functions. This is invaluable when diagnosing high CPU utilization that isn't immediately obvious from `top`, perhaps due to excessive context switching or cache misses. A common mistake is to run `perf` without sufficient permissions or to misinterpret the output, focusing on absolute percentages rather than identifying the functions that consume disproportionate resources relative to their expected workload. Always ensure you have the necessary `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` capabilities or run as root for comprehensive system-wide profiling.

Next, we explore `strace`, a diagnostic tool used to monitor system calls and signals. When an application behaves unexpectedly, hangs, or fails with cryptic errors, `strace` can reveal the underlying system calls it's making and the parameters passed to them. For instance, `strace -p <PID>` will attach to a running process, showing every `open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `execve()`, and other system calls. This is incredibly useful for debugging file permission issues (e.g., an `open()` call failing with `EACCES`), network connection problems (e.g., `connect()` failing), or even understanding why a program is slow (e.g., excessive `stat()` calls on non-existent files). A practical scenario might involve a Python application in a containerized DevOps environment that intermittently fails to write logs. Using `strace` on the Python process could reveal it's trying to write to a non-existent directory or encountering a permission denied error, even if the application logs are unhelpful. Remember that `strace` can introduce significant overhead, so it's best used for short diagnostic bursts or on non-production systems when possible.

For comprehensive historical performance data, `sar` (System Activity Reporter) is indispensable. Part of the `sysstat` package, `sar` collects, reports, and saves system activity information. You can use `sar -u 1 5` to report CPU utilization every second for five intervals, or `sar -r` for memory, `sar -b` for I/O, and `sar -n DEV` for network device statistics. The real power of `sar` comes from its ability to analyze historical data stored in `/var/log/sa/saXX` files, where `XX` is the day of the month. This allows you to review performance trends over hours or days, identifying when a problem started or if it's a recurring pattern. For example, if a cloud instance experiences performance degradation every morning, `sar` data can show if it's correlated with high I/O, CPU, or memory usage during that specific period.

Resource-specific tools like `vmstat`, `iostat`, and `netstat`/`ss` provide focused insights. `vmstat` reports on virtual memory statistics, including processes, memory, paging, block I/O, traps, and CPU activity. Watching the `si` (swap in) and `so` (swap out) columns in `vmstat 1` can quickly indicate if your system is experiencing memory pressure and swapping heavily, which is a major performance killer. `iostat -xz 1` provides detailed CPU and I/O statistics for devices and partitions, showing read/write rates and, critically, the `%util` (percentage of time the device was busy) and `await` (average wait time for I/O requests). High `%util` and `await` values suggest an I/O bottleneck, common in database servers or systems with heavy disk access. Finally, `netstat -tunlp` (or its modern replacement `ss -tunlp`) lists all active network connections, listening ports, and associated processes. This is crucial for verifying service availability, identifying unexpected network traffic, or troubleshooting firewall issues. For instance, if a web service isn't reachable, `ss -tunlp | grep 80` can confirm if the service is actually listening on port 80.

A powerful, yet often overlooked, tool is `lsof` (list open files). Everything in Linux is a file, and `lsof` can list all open files and the processes that opened them. This includes regular files, directories, block devices, character devices, shared libraries, named pipes, and network sockets. `lsof -i :80` will show all processes that have port 80 open (listening or connected), while `lsof /var/log/messages` will show which process is currently writing to the system log. This is incredibly useful for debugging "too many open files" errors, identifying processes holding locks on files, or tracking down network connections. For example, if a database service is failing due to resource limits, `lsof -p <DB_PID> | wc -l` can quickly show the number of open file descriptors, helping you tune `ulimit` settings. Misinterpreting `lsof` output is a common mistake; remember that a file being "open" doesn't always mean it's being actively read or written to, but rather that a process maintains a file descriptor for it.

When approaching performance troubleshooting, adopt a structured methodology. Start broad, using tools like `top`, `vmstat`, `sar` to identify the general area of contention (CPU, memory, I/O, network). Then, narrow down the scope using `pidstat` (from `sysstat`) to identify specific processes, `strace` for system calls, `lsof` for file descriptors, or `perf` for deep CPU profiling. Always formulate hypotheses: "I suspect this application is CPU-bound due to inefficient code," or "I believe the database is slow because of high disk I/O." Test your hypotheses with specific tool outputs. Document your findings and the changes you make. In cloud environments, remember that performance issues can also stem from insufficient instance sizing or network bandwidth limitations, so correlating OS-level metrics with cloud provider metrics (e.g., AWS CloudWatch, Azure Monitor) is crucial. Safe practice dictates that any performance tuning changes should be tested in a staging environment before being applied to production, and always have a rollback plan.

screens.title: Advanced System Monitoring and Performance Tuning
screens.subtitle: Deep tools and structured methods for diagnosing CPU, memory, I/O and network bottlenecks on RHEL

narration.text: In this lesson you will gain practical strategies and tool-based workflows for diagnosing subtle performance problems on Red Hat Enterprise Linux. We focus on kernel-aware profilers, system-call tracing, historical metric collection, device input and output statistics, and how to inspect open files and sockets. You will learn not only the commands but the reasoning: how to form a hypothesis, test it with the right tool, and interpret output that points to C P U, memory, input and output, or network contention. For example, you will see how a profiler pinpoints kernel functions responsible for high system C P U, how strace exposes failing system calls that explain runtime errors, and how sar reveals recurring patterns over days. This knowledge matters because modern cloud and DevOps environments magnify the cost of inefficiency—small misconfigurations or resource leaks cause large user impact. By the end you will be able to choose the right tool for the symptom, collect targeted evidence, and propose safe changes to test in staging before rolling out to production. Consider: what metric would you check first when a service slows only during peak traffic?

keyIdea.title: What you'll master
keyIdea.text: Choosing the right low-overhead tool, forming reproducible hypotheses, correlating OS and cloud metrics, and safely testing tuning changes.

narration.text: These objectives map the skills you'll practice and why they matter. For example, perf helps you find kernel or function-level hotspots that simple process monitors miss. Second, you will interpret device and network statistics from vmstat, iostat, and ss, which lets you detect swapping, input and output saturation, and unexpected listening sockets before they impact users. Third, you will use lsof to inspect open descriptors and sockets to diagnose leaks and misconfigurations, a common cause of gradual degradation. Fourth, you will apply a structured troubleshooting methodology—starting broad and narrowing with focused measurements—so your interventions are evidence-driven and reversible. Each objective combines a command-level skill with decision-making: the 'what to run' is paired with 'what to conclude' and 'how to test safely'. screens.title: Profiling with perf
screens.subtitle: Capture call graphs and hardware events to find CPU hotspots

narration.text: Perf is a kernel-aware profiler that combines hardware counters, kernel events, and user-space call graphs to show where C P U time is consumed. Start with a short system-wide capture, for example recording activity for ten seconds, and then inspect the report to find functions that are disproportionately expensive. The practical value is that perf reveals whether high C P U is due to application logic, kernel work such as input and output or scheduling, or a device driver. In practice you might run a short capture while a load test runs and then use the call graph to isolate a library function or a kernel routine like a filesystem path that dominates time. A common mistake is treating absolute percentages as the full story; instead, compare observed hot functions to expected workload and check call stacks to confirm the true offender. Also ensure you have appropriate privileges: without CAP_SYS_ADMIN you may miss kernel-level events. Example: record a 10 second trace and then open the report to find the top symbols and which processes triggered them. Key takeaway: perf points to the function-level cause so you can decide whether to optimize code, tune kernel parameters, or address a misbehaving driver. What kernel or library function would you expect to see if input and output was the root cause?

keyIdea.title: Perf insight
keyIdea.text: Use perf to move from symptom to function-level evidence — then choose code fix, OS tuning, or driver investigation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › perf Profiling
Command examples
Record a short system-wide profile including call graphs, then report the hottest symbols.
$ sudo perf record -g -a sleep 10
$ sudo perf report
Example
A 10-second capture during a load spike shows a kernel routine dominating time, pointing to I/O or scheduler activity.
Common mistake
Running perf without sufficient privileges or over-interpreting percentages without call-graph context.
Key Takeaway

Perf reveals function-level hotspots — use it to decide if the fix is code optimization, kernel tuning, or hardware investigation.

How to interpret a report
  • Identify top symbols by sample count and their call paths.
  • Map symbols to processes to see whether kernel or user-space dominates.
  • Compare observed hotspots to expected behavior for the workload.
Scenario card
During a database load test, perf shows high samples in a filesystem write path. That suggests I/O rather than pure query CPU; next check iostat for device util and await values.

screens.title: Tracing system calls with strace
screens.subtitle: Observe what a process asks the kernel to do and why it fails

narration.text: Strace is the tool that opens the black box between a process and the kernel. It shows each system call with arguments and return values, which is crucial when applications fail with permissions or missing-file errors, or when they waste time on repeated operations. To use it, attach to a process ID for a short period and inspect calls like open, stat, connect, read, and write. For example, attaching to a Python web server that intermittently fails to write logs may reveal repeated open calls failing with permission denied, something that application logs might not reveal. Keep in mind strace adds measurable overhead; use it briefly or on a staging system. A common misconception is that strace explains C P U hotspots — it does not profile C P U usage as perf does; it reveals functional behavior and failures. In practice you will combine strace's system-call timeline with tools that show resource usage and with lsof to map file descriptors to processes. After a short capture, ask: did the application try to access unexpected paths or repeatedly call a failing syscall? That question guides your fix.

keyIdea.title: Strace insight
keyIdea.text: Use strace for system-call level debugging and to surface permission errors, missing files, or repeated costly syscalls.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › strace Tracing
Attach and observe
# Attach to a running PID briefly (requires privileges)
sudo strace -p 12345

# Or trace a command from start and follow file/network calls
sudo strace -f -o /tmp/trace.log python3 -m http.server 8000
Example output (excerpt)
open("/var/log/app.log", O_WRONLY) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
Interpretation and tips
  • Look for repeated failing calls such as open or connect to find root causes.
  • Use the -f flag to follow child processes and -o to capture logs for post-analysis.
  • Remember strace influences timing — avoid long captures on production traffic.
Pro tip

Combine strace findings with lsof to map failing system calls to open descriptors and confirm the process identity.

screens.title: Investigating open files with lsof
screens.subtitle: List descriptors, sockets, and processes to expose leaks and held resources

narration.text: Lsof lists open files and sockets for processes — critical because in Linux everything is a file. Use it to see which processes hold sockets, logs, or device files, which is especially useful for diagnosing 'too many open files' errors. For example, lsof -i :8000 will show processes with port 8000 open. To diagnose a resource leak, list a process's file descriptors and count them; if the number grows over time, the application likely leaks handles. Another common troubleshooting step is to find which process holds a log or lock file by running lsof against that file name. Remember that an open descriptor doesn't always mean active use; it means the process holds a handle. A common mistake is assuming a high count implies the shell's ulimit; often the service process inherits a different limit from systemd or the container runtime. Use lsof together with ulimit and systemd unit checks. Example scenario: if a containerized database fails with descriptor errors, run lsof -p on its process, count descriptors, and compare to the effective limit to determine whether to increase limits or fix the leak.

keyIdea.title: lsof utility
keyIdea.text: Use lsof to map ports to processes, find who holds files, and detect descriptor leaks by counting open handles.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › lsof Usage
Quick commands
# Show processes with port 8000 open
sudo lsof -i :8000

# Show all open files for a process and count them
sudo lsof -p 12345 | wc -l

# Show which process holds a specific file
sudo lsof /var/log/messages
Scenario
A database container fails with 'Too many open files'. Use lsof -p to count descriptors and confirm whether the service or runtime needs a higher LimitNOFILE.
Interpretation and pitfalls
  • High descriptor counts suggest leaks — track growth over time to confirm.
  • Descriptors held by libraries may be normal; inspect what type (socket, file, pipe) each descriptor represents.
  • Remember systemd and container runtimes may set different limits than your interactive shell.
Key Takeaway

lsof connects symptoms to process identities and descriptor types — vital when diagnosing leaks or held resources.

screens.title: Historical analysis with sar
screens.subtitle: Collect and review system activity logs to find recurring performance patterns

narration.text: Sar, part of the sysstat package, collects and stores historical system activity, which lets you analyze patterns that are invisible in short, live snapshots. Use sar to record C P U, memory, input and output, and network device statistics across hours or days, and consult the saved files in /var/log/sa to see when issues recur. For instance, if a cloud instance slows every morning, sar will show whether input and output, C P U, or memory trends align with that time window, helping you distinguish between periodic jobs and user traffic peaks. Commands like sar -u, sar -r, and sar -b provide targeted views for C P U, memory, and input and output. The power of sar is in correlation: align a sar report with deployment times, cron jobs, or provider-level events to find root causes. A common pitfall is relying only on live tools during an incident; without historical data you may miss the repeating pattern. Practical use: schedule sar collection, and when a slowdown is reported, review the appropriate saXX file to reconstruct the system's behavior over the affected period.

keyIdea.title: Sar advantage
keyIdea.text: Use sar to move from single-incident guesswork to evidence-based trend analysis across days or weeks.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › sar Historical Data
Collect and read
# CPU usage every second for five samples
sar -u 1 5

# Memory report
sar -r 1 5

# I/O activity
sar -b 1 5

# Review stored day file (/var/log/sa/saXX)
sar -f /var/log/sa/sa08 -u
Example
A recurring high I/O spike at 08:00 shown in sar matches a daily backup job, pointing to scheduling adjustments rather than app tuning.
How to use sar effectively
  • Ensure sysstat is configured to collect data at useful intervals and retain files long enough for trend analysis.
  • Correlate sar timestamps with deployment windows, cron schedules, and cloud telemetry.
  • Use targeted sar flags to focus on CPU, memory, or I/O before deep-diving with other tools.
Key Takeaway

Historical sampling with sar is the evidence you need to detect intermittent or scheduled sources of load.

screens.title: vmstat vs iostat — interpreting memory and I/O signals
screens.subtitle: Use vmstat to detect swapping and iostat for device-level saturation

narration.text: Vmstat and iostat answer related, but different, questions. Vmstat reports virtual memory, process, and C P U statistics, and is useful for spotting swapping activity through the si and so columns. Excessive swap in and out indicates memory pressure and a likely service slowdown caused by paging. Iostat reports C P U and device input and output statistics such as percent utilization and average wait times. High device percent utilization and large await values point to device saturation — a classic input and output bottleneck. Use vmstat first to check for system-wide memory pressure, then use iostat to confirm whether specific devices are overloaded. For example, if vmstat shows heavy swap activity concurrent with high iowait in C P U summary, check iostat -xz to find which disk has high %util and long await. One misconception is to treat C P U iowait as always disk-bound; it can also be caused by network storage or driver contention, so correlate device names and kernel activity to be certain. Key takeaway: vmstat tells you system-level pressure, iostat pinpoints the device-level cause. vmstat vs iostat — interpreting memory and I/O signals means use vmstat to see swapping and system pressure; use iostat to identify which device or partition is the bottleneck.. In practical terms, use vmstat to detect swapping and iostat for device-level saturation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory vs Device signals
keyIdea.text: Use vmstat to see swapping and system pressure; use iostat to identify which device or partition is the bottleneck.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › vmstat & iostat
vmstat quick check
# Watch virtual memory and CPU activity
vmstat 1
# Look at columns: si, so, us, sy, id, wa
High si/so indicates swapping. High wa shows processes waiting for I/O; verify with iostat next.
iostat device focus
# Extended device stats with utilization and await
iostat -xz 1
# Check %util and await columns for hotspots
High %util (>80–90%) and increasing await indicate the device cannot keep up with requests and is a bottleneck.
When to use vmstat
First-pass system pressure checks, swapping, CPU wait states.
When to use iostat
Device-level throughput, latency, and utilization analysis.
Key Takeaway

Combine vmstat and iostat: vmstat signals pressure, iostat locates the device offender.

screens.title: ss and netstat for network state
screens.subtitle: Verify listeners, active connections, and the processes behind sockets

narration.text: Ss is the modern, faster replacement for netstat and is essential for examining the system's network state. Use ss -tunlp to list TCP and UDP sockets with the associated process IDs, which helps confirm whether a service is listening on the expected port and which process owns it. This is the first thing to check when a service is reported unreachable: verify that the process actually listens on the port and that the socket state is correct. For troubleshooting unexpected traffic, ss and netstat combined with lsof allow you to map active connections to process names and PIDs. A common misconception is to assume that no listening socket means the service is down; sometimes a firewall or container network mapping hides the listening endpoint from the host view. Therefore always correlate ss output with container runtime and firewall settings. Example: run ss -tunlp and filter for port 80 to ensure the web server is bound as expected. Key takeaway: ss gives you the authoritative picture of network bindings and active sockets on the host. ss and netstat for network state means use ss to confirm service bindings and map sockets to processes before investigating higher-level network problems.. In practical terms, verify listeners, active connections, and the processes behind sockets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Network verification
keyIdea.text: Use ss to confirm service bindings and map sockets to processes before investigating higher-level network problems.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › ss / netstat
Check listening sockets
# Show TCP/UDP sockets with process info
sudo ss -tunlp

# Filter for a specific port
sudo ss -tunlp | grep :80
Confirm the service is bound to the expected interface and port, and note the PID for further inspection.
Correlate with lsof and firewall
  • Use lsof -i :port to verify which process opened a socket.
  • Check firewall and container network settings if the socket is present but unreachable externally.
  • Remember container port mappings may differ from host bindings.
Key Takeaway

ss provides the authoritative host-level view of sockets; always correlate binding with runtime and firewall settings.

screens.title: Structured troubleshooting methodology
screens.subtitle: From broad symptom to focused test and validated change

narration.text: A disciplined troubleshooting methodology prevents wasted effort. Start broad: use top, vmstat, and sar to identify the resource class affected — C P U, memory, input and output, or network. Next, narrow: identify candidate processes with pidstat or top and gather targeted evidence with strace, perf, or lsof depending on the suspected resource. Form a testable hypothesis such as 'I suspect disk input and output is the bottleneck due to heavy writes from process X', then run iostat and perf captures to confirm. Test your hypothesis in a staging environment or during a controlled window, document the change and metrics before and after, and always have a rollback plan. Correlate OS-level evidence with cloud provider metrics to determine whether the issue is instance sizing or local saturation. A common error is to change configuration in production without a rollback plan. Good practice keeps changes reversible and data-driven. Example workflow: observe high iowait, identify process with high write activity, use perf to check kernel activity, and finally adjust input and output scheduler or resize storage. Which hypothesis will you run first when the next slowdown is reported?

keyIdea.title: Methodology
keyIdea.text: Observe, hypothesize, gather targeted evidence, test in staging, and document changes with rollback plans.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Troubleshooting Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Observe: top, vmstat, sar to classify the resource affected.
  2. Narrow: pidstat, top, ss to find candidate processes and sockets.
  3. Evidence: perf for CPU, iostat for devices, strace for syscalls, lsof for descriptors.
  4. Test: validate hypothesis in staging and measure before/after.
  5. Document & rollback: record changes and have a rollback plan.
Scenario example
A web application shows high response latency. Observe: vmstat shows rising swap and iowait. Narrow: pidstat shows process PID 234 with heavy IO. Evidence: iostat shows disk util at 99% and high await. Action: test in staging by increasing disk throughput or resizing instance. Document results and roll back if user-facing errors increase.
Key Takeaway

Follow a repeatable workflow: observe, narrow, gather evidence, test in staging, document and rollback.

screens.title: Hands-on lab: Python web server and load
screens.subtitle: Simulate load, monitor with vmstat, iostat, sar, then inspect with strace and lsof

narration.text: This lab reproduces a common cloud scenario: a simple web server that experiences slowdowns under load. First, start the Python web server and note its PID. Then generate concurrency with a load tool to create measurable pressure. While the load runs, record vmstat and iostat outputs to detect swapping or device saturation. Use sar to capture short historical samples. When you observe symptom spikes, attach strace briefly to the server PID to see failing system calls or excessive stat/open calls. Finally, run lsof to confirm how many descriptors the server holds and whether sockets are opened as expected. The supplied shell template automates setup and tear-down so you can safely reproduce the issue in a lab. Important safety: use short durations for strace and run perf or strace with appropriate privileges in a staging environment. After the exercise, formulate a hypothesis: is it C P U-bound, input and output-bound, or due to file descriptor leaks? Document evidence and a reversible mitigation. Which measurement convinced you of the root cause? Hands-on lab: Python web server and load means reproduce an end-to-end slowdown and use command outputs to form and test hypotheses about cpu, i/o, or descriptor issues.. In practical terms, simulate load, monitor with vmstat, iostat, sar, then inspect with strace and lsof. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab purpose
keyIdea.text: Reproduce an end-to-end slowdown and use command outputs to form and test hypotheses about CPU, I/O, or descriptor issues.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Lab Walkthrough
Starter commands (run on RHEL)
mkdir ~/web_app && cd ~/web_app
echo "Hello from Cohortia!" > index.html
nohup python3 -m http.server 8000 &
echo $! > ~/web_app/server.pid

# From a load client
ab -n 1000 -c 10 http://:8000/

# Monitoring samples
vmstat 1 5
iostat -xz 1 5
sar -u 1 5
When done, kill the server and clean the directory to leave the host tidy.
Inspection steps
  • Find the server PID and attach strace for a few seconds to observe system calls.
  • Use lsof -i :8000 to confirm listening sockets and lsof -p PID to count descriptors.
  • Compare vmstat and iostat outputs during the load to identify memory or I/O pressure.
Key Takeaway

This reproducible lab ties tools together so you can practice forming evidence-based hypotheses and safe remediations.

screens.title: Correlating OS metrics with cloud telemetry
screens.subtitle: Decide between code fixes, OS tuning, or instance resizing

narration.text: OS-level tools show what is happening on the host, but cloud provider metrics show whether the problem is local capacity or the instance type. When you see high device utilization or consistent C P U saturation on the host, compare the timestamps to provider telemetry such as instance C P U credits, network throughput, or disk bandwidth metrics. If host sar and iostat show device saturation while provider metrics show the instance disk throughput capped, the fix is likely resizing storage or instance type. Conversely, if only the host shows kernel-side contention or a leaking process, the remediation is local tuning or code changes. A useful pattern is to gather sar/vmstat/iostat data, then pull provider metrics for the same window and align them to confirm whether cloud limits or local saturation cause the symptom. Avoid changing instance type without evidence; it may mask an application-level resource leak. Document the correlation and use staging tests before any production resizing. What evidence would shift your recommendation from tuning to resizing? keyIdea.title: Correlation principle
keyIdea.text: Align OS metrics with provider telemetry to choose between code fixes, OS tuning, or scaling resources.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › OS & Cloud Correlation
What to align
  • Sar/vmstat timestamps with provider CPU, disk, and network metrics.
  • iostat device utilization with cloud disk throughput and IOPS limits.
  • ss/lsof evidence with load balancer metrics to confirm external traffic patterns.
If both OS and provider metrics show saturation at the same time, resizing or higher throughput storage may be needed. If only the OS shows unusual kernel activity, prefer local investigation and tuning.
Decision checklist
Evidence of device %util near saturation across the timeframe → consider storage resizing.
Kernel functions dominating CPU in perf report without provider CPU cap → investigate drivers or code.
Growing open file descriptors in lsof with stable provider metrics → fix application leak or ulimit settings in the runtime.
Key Takeaway

Use aligned evidence to choose the correct mitigation: tuning, code fix, or cloud resizing, and validate changes in staging.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safe tuning practices
screens.subtitle: Permissions, overhead, inherited limits, and change control

narration.text: When tuning or diagnosing, several recurring mistakes undermine confidence in results. First, running tools without sufficient permissions can produce incomplete data — perf and some syscalls require elevated capabilities. Second, some tools add overhead: strace can change timing and perf sampling may need careful durations; always prefer short captures on production. Third, assume that shell ulimit equals the service's effective limit; services launched by systemd or container runtimes may have different limits, so check unit files and container runtime flags. Fourth, make changes without a rollback plan; any tuning that affects input and output schedulers, kernel parameters, or resource limits should be tested in staging first. Finally, misinterpreting open files as active use leads to false conclusions — an open descriptor may be idle. Best practice: document the baseline metrics, take time-stamped evidence, make one change at a time in staging, and measure the effect. After a successful change, record the outcome and the rollback steps to keep your production environment safe. What rollback will you plan for the next tuning you propose? keyIdea.title: Safe tuning
keyIdea.text: Avoid permission blindspots, limit tool overhead, verify effective limits, and always test changes in staging with a rollback plan.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Pitfalls & Safety
Frequent mistakes
  • Insufficient privileges lead to incomplete data from perf or strace.
  • Long strace sessions on production skew timing and hide true behavior.
  • Assuming interactive shell limits apply to services launched by systemd or container runtimes.
Safe practice checklist
Always record baseline metrics with timestamps before making changes.
Test changes in staging and apply one change at a time for clear attribution.
Prepare a rollback plan and document results.
Key Takeaway

Good measurement plus staged, reversible changes keeps production safe while improving performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to carry forward

narration.text: These three compact concepts will anchor your troubleshooting practice. First, perf provides function-level profiling that reveals whether C P U time is spent in application code or kernel paths, helping you choose between code optimization or system-level fixes. Second, strace and lsof expose what a process requests from the kernel and which files or sockets it holds, which is essential for diagnosing permission errors, stuck resources, or descriptor leaks. Third, sar, vmstat, and iostat give you both historical and device-level views; use sar for trends, vmstat to spot swapping and system pressure, and iostat to identify which disk or partition is saturated. Keep these tools as complementary lenses rather than alternatives, always correlate their outputs, and validate any tuning in staging with a rollback plan. narration.text: Keep these actionable reminders handy when you troubleshoot. First, form a clear hypothesis: pick the resource class and an expected cause before running heavy tools. Second, collect targeted evidence with the right tool — use perf for C P U hotspots, iostat for device bottlenecks, and strace for failing syscalls — then correlate results. Third, always validate changes in a staging environment and have a rollback plan; this keeps production safe while allowing iterative tuning. These three rules reduce guesswork, speed diagnostic cycles, and improve the chance that your first mitigation will be correct.
